questions.prompt: In traditional letterpress printing, which part of the type carries ink onto the paper?
questions.hint: Imagine which parts of an inked rubber stamp touch the paper.
questions.explanation: Letterpress prints from raised, inked surfaces. Recessed ink belongs to intaglio; backing and spaces are not the intended printing surfaces. Job compares the emerging detail of dawn to a seal shaping clay, within God’s challenge to Job. The comparison concerns an impression, not an ancient prediction of printing.
questions.authorFinding: A seal can itself be recessed, so do not claim Job establishes the raised geometry of letterpress. Test whether the stamp analogy helps beyond the seal reading.

questions.prompt: According to Sarah Bradford’s biography, who used “Go Down, Moses” to identify herself to people escaping slavery?
questions.hint: She was known as a conductor on the Underground Railroad.
questions.explanation: Bradford’s 1886 biography describes Tubman singing the spiritual so that people waiting in hiding would recognize their returning guide. The song draws on Moses’ demand to Pharaoh; the displayed passage contains that demand. All four choices were women involved in opposing slavery, but Tubman is the person in this account. The question attributes this reported episode to its source rather than generalizing that spirituals routinely encoded escape directions.
questions.authorFinding: Replaces held Eratosthenes-shadow-measurement inference with a documented later use of a biblical demand. Four real women abolitionists prevent a gender giveaway. Conductor clue is familiar but may repeat what the stem already implies; benefit remains unmeasured. Library of Congress indexed material supports this specific account and warns broader song-code claims are debated; direct LOC page fetches returned403. Full Bradford primary biography was read successfully, including the recognition-signal scene. Historical primary text contains dated racial language and inflated rescue totals: neither is reproduced or adopted. Exodus5 alternative was read but rejected to avoid overlapping existing History straw question; Exodus8 range used instead. Do not claim an exclusive single-verse origin for the song.
questions.concept: Harriet Tubman and the Go Down Moses identification signal
questions.coordinatorFinding: Supernatural shadow movement does not help derive city baseline. Retain as uncertain pairing.

coordinatorDecision.caveat: Tubman remains conditional on primary Bradford attribution as written and independent source check.

questions.prompt: Why was straw mixed into traditional sun-dried mud bricks?
answers: To help limit cracking as they dried
To make the brick surfaces smoother
questions.hint: Small fibres help a drying lump hold together.
questions.explanation: Straw helps mud bricks shrink more uniformly as they dry, limiting cracking. It does not waterproof the brick, smooth its surface, or increase its density. Pharaoh increases the burden on enslaved workers by withdrawing supplied straw while retaining their brick quota. The useful material detail is part of that oppression, not an endorsement of it.
questions.authorFinding: Easy opener candidate. Do not generalize to permanent reinforcing strength: NPS specifically distinguishes more uniform shrinkage from added long-term strength. Scripture names the ingredient but not its drying function.

questions.prompt: On wooden ships, what was oakum used for?
answers: Binding the anchor to its chain
questions.hint: Think of the gaps through which seawater could enter a hull.
questions.explanation: Oakum consists of rope fibres driven into plank seams; pitch then helps seal the joints against water. The alternatives are other conceivable uses of fibrous material, not the documented caulking role. Genesis specifies coating the ark with pitch inside and out. It does not mention oakum or identify the later shipbuilding technique.
questions.authorFinding: Concrete waterproofing analogy, not proof Noah used oakum. Keep pitch and fibres distinct. Hint adds the likely entry point for water without using the correct answer wording.

questions.prompt: What does the expression “the writing is on the wall” usually signal today?
questions.hint: Think of a company losing its biggest customers month after month.
questions.explanation: The expression means visible warning of an unfavorable outcome. Its history runs back to the writing interpreted in Daniel5, which announces the end of Belshazzar’s rule. The reading gives the function of the warning; the modern idiom extends that idea to ordinary situations such as a struggling business. It does not mean a secret instruction, an official authorization, or an unsupported accusation.
questions.authorFinding: Replaces held winding-aqueduct versus straight-highway analogy. The passage supplies an actual example of the idiom’s origin rather than a loosely matched object. Four possible functions of a message; accusation is a plausible reading trap because the king is found wanting, but the idiom signals an unfavorable future. Independent business example is an original clue, benefit unmeasured. Easy language-history item; coordinator should assess History taxonomy versus Media. Display includes the interpretation; opening feast/hand/wall verses1–6 and outcomecontext22–30 were separately read. Do not present Daniel’s scales as a physical measurement or the banquet as an archaeological proof claim.
questions.concept: Historical origin and modern meaning of writing on the wall
questions.coordinatorFinding: Held: weak boats/shade/pressure distractors make gradient conspicuous; straight-highway passage versus winding route creates confusion. Replace pairing or asked question, not merely hedge.

coordinatorDecision.caveat: Easy candidate; preserve author and source caveats and test reading/hint contribution.
